blocks.text: Before a client can talk to any MCP server, it first has to know that server exists. That sounds obvious, but it is a real step, and different tools solve it in different ways.
Some clients read a small config file listing every server they should connect to. Others pull from a registry, or let a person type in a connection command by hand.
This lesson walks through all three discovery paths, looks closely at the shape of a typical server config, and covers why a newly discovered server still needs to earn your trust.
1. What Discovery Actually Means
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441013284-428334775.png

Discovery is simply the step where a host application decides which servers it should try to connect to. It happens before initialization, before capability negotiation, before anything protocol level even starts.
Without discovery, a client has no list of servers to reach out to at all. It would just sit there with no tools, no resources, and nothing to offer a model.

blocks.title: Discovery is a client side concern
blocks.content: MCP itself does not define one single required discovery mechanism. Each host application, a desktop app, an IDE plugin, a coding agent, is free to choose how it builds its own list of servers.

blocks.text: That freedom is why the same server can look slightly different depending on which client you add it to. The underlying protocol conversation, once connected, stays identical either way.
2. The Three Common Discovery Paths
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441013285-465586762.png
In practice, almost every MCP client falls back on one of three patterns to build its server list. Knowing all three helps you recognize which one any given tool is using.

items: A configuration file listing servers by name, with how to start or reach each one.
A registry, a central catalog a client can query or browse for available servers.
Manual entry, where a person types in a connection command or a URL directly.

blocks.text: These are not mutually exclusive. Many real clients support a config file as the default path and manual entry as a fallback for one off testing.
A single client can even mix all three at once, a base config file, an optional registry lookup, and a quick manual add for something experimental.
3. Anatomy of a Typical mcp.json File
The most common config file pattern uses a top level object, usually called mcpServers, mapping a short server name to its connection details.
Notice the two entries look nothing alike. One describes a command to run locally, the other describes a URL to reach out to over the network.
4. Naming Servers Inside a Config
The key next to each entry, local-files or weather-remote in the example above, is just a human readable label the client uses internally. It has no protocol meaning of its own.
Good naming still matters a lot in practice. A vague name like server1 makes it much harder to debug which server a failing tool call actually came from.

items: Use a name that describes what the server does, not where it happens to live.
Keep names stable once tools or prompts start referring to them.
Avoid reusing the same name for two very different servers across projects.

blocks.text: A quick rename before sharing a config with a teammate can save both of you real confusion later.
5. Local Servers in a Config, the stdio Shape

blocks.alt: Local Servers in a Config, the stdio Shape
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441013285-287865439.png
A local server entry tells the client how to start a brand new process on the same machine. The client will spawn it and talk to it over standard input and output.
The command and args fields together are exactly what you would type on a command line yourself. The client just runs that command as a child process instead of a person doing it.
6. Remote Servers in a Config, the URL Shape
A remote server entry looks completely different. Instead of a command to launch, it holds a URL the client should open a connection to.

There is no process for the client to manage here at all. The server is already running somewhere else, and the client simply needs a way to reach it and, often, a credential to prove it is allowed to.
7. Local versus Remote, Why Discovery Differs
These two shapes exist because local and remote servers need fundamentally different information to be reachable at all.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Local, stdio server","Remote server"],"rows":[["What the client needs","A command and arguments to run","A URL and, usually, a credential"],["Who starts the server","The client, as a child process","Someone else, already running"],["Typical trust boundary","Whatever runs on your machine","Whoever operates that remote host"]]}

blocks.text: 8. Environment Variables and Secrets in Config
Both local and remote entries often need small bits of secret data, an API key, a folder path, a bearer token, to actually function correctly.
For local servers this usually lives in an env block passed to the spawned process. For remote servers it is more often a header sent with every request.

blocks.title: Config files are not a safe place for long lived secrets
blocks.content: A config file listing a raw API key is easy to accidentally commit to a shared repository. Many teams instead point the env or headers value at an environment variable reference rather than a literal secret.

items: Prefer a reference to an environment variable over a literal secret in the file itself.
Keep any config file holding real secrets out of shared version control.
Rotate a token immediately if a config file containing it is ever exposed by mistake.

blocks.text: 9. Registries, Discovery Beyond a Static File

blocks.alt: Registries, Discovery Beyond a Static File
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441013286-812605969.png
A registry is a step up from a hand maintained config file. It is a catalog a client can query, browse, or search to find servers it did not already know about.
Instead of you typing in every server yourself, the client asks the registry, here is what a user is looking for, and gets back a list of matching candidates.

items: A registry can list many more servers than any one person would ever configure by hand.
A registry entry usually still resolves down to the same command or URL shape seen in a config file.
A registry adds an extra actor, the registry operator, whose trustworthiness now also matters.

blocks.title: A registry listing is a claim, not a guarantee
blocks.content: Anyone can publish a listing to an open registry. The listing itself is only a starting point, the same validation steps covered later in this lesson still apply in full.

blocks.text: 10. Manual Entry, the Escape Hatch
Sometimes a server is brand new, still being built, or simply not worth adding to a shared config file yet. Manual entry covers exactly that case.
Under the hood this usually just writes the same kind of entry you would see in a config file. Manual entry is more about who is deciding to add the server, not about a different underlying format.
11. From Discovery to First Connection
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441013286-735938090.png
Once a client has a server entry, whether from a config file, a registry, or manual entry, discovery itself is finished. What follows next is the actual connection attempt.

items: For a local entry, the client spawns the process and opens stdio pipes to it.
For a remote entry, the client opens a network connection to the given URL.
Either way, the client then sends the initialize request as the very first message.

blocks.text: Discovery only hands the client an address or a command. It says nothing yet about whether that server is safe or well behaved.
That gap, between having an address and actually earning trust, is exactly what the rest of this lesson focuses on.
12. Why a Discovered Server Cannot Be Trusted Blindly

blocks.alt: Why a Discovered Server Cannot Be Trusted Blindly
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441013286-746628383.png
Just because a server showed up in a config file, a registry result, or a typed in URL does not mean it is safe to hand real data to.

A config file could have been edited by someone else on a shared machine. A registry listing could be outdated, misleading, or outright malicious. A manually typed URL could simply be a typo pointing somewhere unexpected.

blocks.title: Discovery answers where, not whether
blocks.content: Finding a server only tells a client where to try connecting. Whether that server is the one it claims to be, and whether it behaves safely, is a separate question that discovery alone never answers.

blocks.text: 13. Validating a Server After Discovery
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785441013287-356147688.png
Before a client hands a discovered server any real trust, it should check a few basic things during and right after the initialize handshake.

items: Does the server respond to initialize at all, within a reasonable time.
Does the serverInfo name and version look like what the config or registry claimed.
Do the declared capabilities match what the client actually expected to use.
For remote servers, is the connection using a secure transport, not plain unencrypted traffic.

blocks.text: A mismatch here is worth stopping for
If the returned serverInfo name does not match what the config or registry claimed, treat that as a real warning sign, not a minor detail to shrug off.
14. Practical Trust Checks Before First Real Use
A responsible client goes a bit further than just checking the handshake succeeded. It also gives a person a chance to review what a new server can actually do.

items: List the tools a newly connected server exposes before letting a model call any of them.
Warn a user the first time a brand new server, not seen before, is about to be used.
Flag remote servers separately from local ones, since the trust boundary is different.
Let a user revoke or remove a server easily if it starts behaving oddly.

blocks.text: None of these checks are exotic. They are closer to the same caution you would already apply before installing a browser extension from an unfamiliar source.
15. Keeping Discovery Config Manageable Over Time
A config file that starts with two servers can easily grow to a dozen or more as a project matures. Left unmanaged, this becomes hard to audit.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Habit","Why it helps"],"rows":[["Remove entries for servers you no longer use","Fewer stale credentials and processes lying around"],["Group local and remote entries visually","Makes the differing trust boundary obvious at a glance"],["Review the config after adding any new server","Catches copy paste mistakes before they cause confusion"]]}

blocks.text: A little routine housekeeping here goes a long way toward keeping the whole discovery layer trustworthy, not just the servers you added most recently.
Treat the config file itself as part of your project, worth reviewing in the same way you would review any other change.

For notes-local, the client will spawn node with that script path as a child process, then talk to it over stdio.

In both cases, the very next step after connecting is the same, send initialize, check the response, and only then trust the server enough to list its tools.
Common Mistakes

items: Treating a server appearing in a config file as automatically trustworthy, with no validation at all.
Storing a raw API key or bearer token directly in a shared config file instead of an environment reference.
Assuming a remote server entry works the same way as a local one, and forgetting it needs a secure transport.
Never reviewing a config file as it grows, until it holds several servers nobody remembers adding.
Letting a registry listing skip the same initialize and capability checks a manually added server would go through.
Reusing a vague server name across very different projects, making later debugging far harder than it needs to be.

blocks.text: Practice
Write your own small mcp.json with one local server, using a command and args, and one remote server, using a url and a header.
Then trace through, on paper, exactly what a client would do with each entry, from reading the config through sending the first initialize request.

items: Stretch goal one: add a second local server and give both local entries clearly distinct, descriptive names.
Stretch goal two: write down three checks you would want a client to run before trusting your remote entry.

blocks.text: Key Takeaway
Discovery is just the first step, a client learning which servers exist through a config file, a registry, or manual entry. It answers where to look, nothing more.
Whether a discovered server deserves real trust is a separate question, answered only after a successful handshake and a few sensible checks, not by the mere fact that it showed up in a list.
